articles.title: Lula resgata Hino da Independência em atos na Paulista em disputa por símbolos nacionais: 'para saberem que não cabemos no quintal de ninguém' | G1
articles.standfirst: Composição foi tocada no último ato de campanha antes do segundo turno no sábado (24) e na comemoração da vitória do presidente no domingo (25).
articles.summary: Composição foi tocada no último ato de campanha antes do segundo turno no sábado (24) e na comemoração da vitória do presidente no domingo (25).
articles.body:
No último ato de campanha antes do segundo turno e, no dia seguinte, na comemoração da vitória, o presidente Lula ( PT ) escolheu o mesmo símbolo para embalar dois momentos decisivos da eleição: o Hino da Independência do Brasil.

Diante de milhares de apoiadores na Avenida Paulista, em São Paulo, Lula pediu que a música fosse tocada e, no domingo (25), explicou o motivo: queria que seus adversários soubessem que o Brasil “não cabe no quintal de ninguém”.

A escolha acontece em meio à disputa política em torno do significado do termo "soberania" e de símbolos nacionais, como a bandeira brasileira, o verde e amarelo e os hinos patrióticos, que ganharam força como marcas de identificação da extrema-direita nos últimos anos.

Ao recorrer ao Hino da Independência nos dois atos, Lula leva para o centro de sua celebração eleitoral uma referência à liberdade e à soberania do país.

🔎 Composto pelo Imperador D. Pedro I, em 1822, a letra do Hino da Independência foi escrita pelo poeta Evaristo da Veiga. A composição comemora a declaração de independência do país de Portugal e foi usada como hino nacional do Brasil até 1831.

Lula discursa na avenida Paulista — Foto: Reuters

No sábado (24), Lula desfilou em um trio elétrico pela Paulista ao lado da esposa, Janja, e de aliados políticos, entre eles os ex-ministros Fernando Haddad, Marina Silva e Simone Tebet. A campanha e o próprio presidente descreveram o ato como um dos maiores já realizados na avenida. No auge do ato, 14 dos 18 quarteirões estavam ocupados por manifestantes.

Quando o Hino da Independência começou a tocar, uma pequena parcela do público pareceu estranhar a escolha. Algumas pessoas se entreolharam, mas a reação rapidamente mudou à medida que o refrão avançou.

“Brava gente brasileira, longe vá, temor servil. Ou ficar a Pátria livre, ou morrer pelo Brasil”, cantaram os manifestantes emocionados.

No domingo (25), durante o discurso em que celebrou a vitória no segundo turno, Lula pediu que o hino fosse tocado novamente. “Ontem eu fiquei emocionado, e eu quero pedir para outra vez tocar o Hino da Independência. Para eles saberem que nós não cabemos no quintal de ninguém”, afirmou.

O significado de soberania também virou alvo de disputa política durante a campanha eleitoral. De um lado, Lula associa o tema à autonomia do Brasil diante de pressões de outros países. Do outro, o adversário Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL ) usou o termo para falar de segurança pública, segundo a cientista política Tathiana Chicarino, coordenadora do curso de graduação em Sociologia e Política da FESPSP.

“Para essa frente democrática, soberania significa não interferência de uma potência global, como são os Estados Unidos, em questões domésticas, sejam elas eleitorais, sejam elas sobre condução de assuntos comerciais. Então, eu faço comércio contigo, eu não tenho que ceder ao que ele deseja só pelo desejo e pela força desse país”, afirmou.

Já a extrema-direita, segundo a cientista política, apresentou outra leitura do conceito durante a campanha. Ela cita as declarações de Flávio Bolsonaro, que associou soberania ao direito de andar pelas ruas em segurança.

“Ele trata soberania em termos de segurança pública e tenta dissociar desses elementos de relações internacionais, sobre essa geopolítica”, disse.

Apoiadores de Lula acompanham apuração na Avenida Paulista — Foto: GABRIEL SILVA

Nesse cenário, o Hino da Independência ajuda a conectar o discurso de Lula à ideia de autonomia nacional, avalia a cientista política. Para ela, o refrão conhecido e direto dá força à mensagem.

“É um hino que todo mundo sabe cantar, tem um refrão bastante contundente e muito direto, muito claro”, afirmou. “O uso desse hino dá esse enquadramento para essa discussão de soberania que o presidente Lula tem feito.”

Tathiana também vê a disputa pelos símbolos nacionais como parte do debate democrático. Para ela, bandeira, cores e referências patrióticas não devem ser tratados como propriedade de um único campo político.

“Patriotismo nacional e defesa do Brasil não são bandeiras exclusivas da extrema-direita, nunca foram. Esses são termos políticos que estão sempre em disputa”, afirmou.

A associação entre símbolos nacionais, como os hinos patrióticos, a bandeira brasileira, a camisa da Seleção e as cores verde e amarelo, e a extrema-direita antecede a chegada de Jair Bolsonaro à Presidência.

Segundo a cientista política Tathiana Chicarino, essa disputa ganhou força nas manifestações de 2013 e nos protestos pelo impeachment de Dilma Rousseff, em 2015 e 2016, e se consolidou com a eleição de Bolsonaro, em 2018.

“Essas disputas remontam ali a 2013, uma disputa da rua. Isso vai aparecer em termos de cores. Então, a gente vai começar a identificar o verde e amarelo como sendo de um campo e o vermelho de outro”, afirmou.

Para a pesquisadora, a associação entre as cores e campos políticos também reflete uma polarização que vai além das diferenças partidárias.

“Isso tem a ver com essa intensificação de uma polarização afetiva, que não é uma polarização partidária apenas, ou política. Ela é afetiva: eu não vejo o outro e não chego perto do outro. É uma disputa intensa com o outro, quase como nessa simbologia de camisas diferentes, de cores diferentes e de times diferentes, pensando nessa lógica mais de futebol”, disse.

Apoiadores do candidato à Presidência, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), participam do ato Bloco do 22, realizado neste domingo, 18, na Avenida Paulista, em São Paulo. — Foto: LUIZA FLORENZANO/MODUSFOCUS/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

Com Bolsonaro, esses símbolos se consolidaram como marcas de identificação do bolsonarismo. Durante a campanha presidencial de 2026, apoiadores de Lula também tentaram reivindicar as cores nacionais.

Em 17 de outubro, a oito dias do segundo turno, o deputado federal André Janones (Rede-MG), criador do canal de WhatsApp “Exército do Lula”, lançou uma missão para os seguidores: publicar fotos nas redes sociais usando verde e amarelo e fazendo o “L” com as mãos, em referência ao petista.

A iniciativa é um exemplo da tentativa de romper a associação automática entre as cores nacionais e um único campo político. Tathiana cita movimentos desse tipo ao avaliar que a disputa pode fazer com que mais pessoas se sintam à vontade para usar esses símbolos sem serem identificadas com determinada posição política.

A cientista política também diferencia duas formas de nacionalismo: uma excludente , que delimita quem pertence ou não à comunidade nacional, e outra inclusiva , capaz de reunir pessoas com identidades e diferenças diversas.

“Existe um nacionalismo que pode ganhar contornos bastante xenofóbicos. Um nacionalismo que é fechado, que delimita quem está dentro e quem está fora. Então, bastante excludente”, afirmou.

Em contraposição, ela descreve um nacionalismo que não exige uniformidade para criar um sentimento de pertencimento ao país.

“Mas a gente pode ter um nacionalismo mais inclusivo, que, de alguma maneira, foi o que a gente foi construindo em termos de nacionalismo no pós-ditadura, com a redemocratização. Então, ser brasileiro ou se sentir brasileiro é mais do que ter nascido brasileiro”, disse.

Para Tathiana, essa ideia permite compartilhar referências nacionais sem apagar as diferenças entre os brasileiros. “Eu posso ter esse nacionalismo que é inclusivo, que é diferente, é diverso, é regionalizado. Mas, ao mesmo tempo, a gente consegue perceber algo que nos une.”

Lula segura a Constituição e a bandeira do Brasil em ato na Paulista — Foto: LUIZA FLORENZANO/MODUSFOCUS/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

articles.title: Trump ends visa-free entry for Chinese nationals over birth tourism in Pacific island
articles.summary: The Trump administration has suspended a programme that allowed Chinese nationals to visit a US territory in the Pacific for up to 14 days without a visa,
articles.body: The Trump administration has suspended a programme that allowed Chinese nationals to visit a US territory in the Pacific for up to 14 days without a visa, citing concerns over national security, illegal immigration and possible espionage.The decision affects the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), a US territory in the western Pacific. The programme allowed eligible Chinese visitors to enter after screening by US Customs and Border Protection, without obtaining a visa through a US consulate.US Senator Mike Lee, a Republican from Utah, announced the suspension in a post on X on Monday, crediting Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin with ending what he described as a loophole for Chinese birth tourism."I’m very pleased to report that @SecMullinDHS at @DHSgov just CLOSED Joe Biden’s loophole for Chinese birth tourism for which we sounded the alarm earlier this year," Lee said."America is not a nursery for the CCP to steal citizenship. Thank you, President Trump!" he added.Lee also drew attention to an April post by Fox News correspondent Bill Melugin, who reported that four Republican senators had urged the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to shut down the programme. They argued that some Chinese visitors were using it to have children in US territory and obtain American citizenship for them through birthright citizenship.Why the US has suspended the programmeAn official DHS notice announced the suspension of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands Economic Vitality and Security Travel Authorization Program, known as EVS-TAP.Introduced in 2024, the programme allowed prescreened Chinese nationals to visit the territory without a visa for stays of up to 14 days, subject to specific conditions. It was designed to support tourism and business travel while maintaining security checks.The department said more than 3,000 Chinese nationals entered the territory through the scheme in the 2025 fiscal year. Their applications were screened by US Customs and Border Protection rather than by consular officers at the State Department.The notice said the United States faced "evolving and sophisticated threats" and that the number of Chinese nationals entering through the programme created "a significant risk to the security and law enforcement interests of the United States."It added, "While the program was intended to facilitate economic travel and enhance security over the prior parole policy, this volume of visa-exempt entries presents unacceptable security and law enforcement risks."The suspension applies to new applicants as well as travellers who already hold authorisations under the programme. Chinese nationals who are already in the CNMI legally under EVS-TAP will be allowed to remain until their authorised period of stay expires. They will need a visa for future visits.Espionage, illegal travel and birth tourism concernsThe DHS notice raised concerns that the programme was being exploited for purposes beyond tourism and business travel.One major concern was the possibility of espionage and intelligence gathering targeting US defence infrastructure in the Indo-Pacific. The CNMI and nearby Guam are strategically important because the region hosts military facilities central to American defence operations.The department cited cases in which Chinese nationals were "convicted of conspiring" to transport other Chinese nationals illegally from the CNMI to Guam. One case involved nine people, while another involved seven. According to the notice, most of those individuals were "later encountered in or near sensitive military installations".The department also raised concerns about birth tourism, in which foreign visitors travel to a country primarily to give birth there so their children can obtain citizenship under its laws.US authorities argued that the programme could be used by visitors seeking American citizenship for children born in the territory despite having no lasting ties to the United States. The notice also warned that birth tourism could put pressure on local medical facilities and create additional security risks.Other concerns included organised criminal networks, money laundering and labour abuses allegedly linked to businesses connected to China operating in the territory.The suspension does not automatically establish that all Chinese visitors using the programme engaged in illegal activity. Instead, the department said the identified risks justified ending visa-free access while it reassessed the scheme.What happens to Chinese travellers Chinese nationals seeking to visit the Northern Mariana Islands for business or tourism will now need to obtain an appropriate non-immigrant visa before travelling, unless they qualify for another lawful exemption.The suspension does not bring back the previous parole policy for Chinese nationals seeking entry to the territory. That policy was discontinued on February 20, 2025.The DHS acknowledged that ending the programme could hurt local businesses that depend on visitors from China and cause inconvenience or financial losses for prospective travellers. However, it said national security, immigration enforcement and law enforcement concerns took priority.The department will review the programme in consultation with the Departments of State and the Interior to assess the risks and consider whether safeguards could address them.The decision highlights the challenge facing the Northern Mariana Islands, which has sought to attract Chinese tourists and business visitors while remaining part of a strategically important US military region in the Pacific.You use AI every day. articles.title: France unrest: Why Macron govt's proposed law for action against rioters is facing criticism
articles.summary: A proposed French law that would require rioters to pay up to €10,000 ($11,150) for the damage they cause has drawn criticism from human rights groups and
articles.body: A proposed French law that would require rioters to pay up to €10,000 ($11,150) for the damage they cause has drawn criticism from human rights groups and some lawyers, who argue that it threatens the fundamental democratic right to protest.President Emmanuel Macron’s government, facing pressure to contain France’s worst unrest in years, says the proposed law is necessary to compensate victims of vandalism that often accompanies protests, including the looting and rioting witnessed on October 17.Critics, however, argue that the draft legislation is so broadly worded that peaceful demonstrators who happen to be near incidents of violence could also be held legally liable and face prosecution.“Violence and property damage can occur on the fringes of a protest without the vast majority of peaceful, legitimate demonstrators having any involvement,” said Hanna Bouchareb, a Paris-based lawyer who represented some of those accused of rioting in fast-track trials following the October 17 unrest, Reuters reported.“It’s very problematic because it undermines the right to protest,” Bouchareb added.Interior minister Laurent Nunez, who offered to resign last week after security forces struggled to contain the unrest but was asked by Macron to remain in his post, rejected claims that the proposed law "undermines" the principle of individual accountability.“The change introduced by this draft law is the establishment of joint responsibility, not collective responsibility,” Nunez told broadcaster TF1.However, France’s Human Rights League (LDH) and a group of trade unionists disputed that distinction. In a column published in Le Monde over the weekend, they called for the proposed legislation to be scrapped.What does the draft bill sayThe draft legislation stipulates that anyone who knowingly belongs to a group would be held jointly liable for any damage caused by any member of that group.It also empowers the state to seize welfare benefits from those convicted under the law, or from their parents if the offenders are minors, to help cover the costs of the damage.French businesses and retailers say they have suffered losses worth millions of euros due to looting and vandalism, as well as being forced to close their shops and board up windows during protests.Police tactics draw renewed scrutinyPolice faced accusations of excessive force in 2020 during anti-government “yellow vest” demonstrations. At the time, a proposed law restricting the circulation of images of police officers under certain circumstances also drew criticism before being watered down.In recent weeks, protesters have again accused police of using "heavy-handed" tactics against student demonstrators, while lawyers, including Bouchareb, have raised concerns about the fast-tracked convictions of some people accused of rioting.Supporters of the proposed legislation point to surveys indicating broad public backing for the measure. Marine Le Pen’s National Rally (RN), a far-right party and a leading contender in next year’s presidential election, has argued for even tougher measures.You use AI every day. articles.title: US charges 48 non-citizens over election-related crimes in Pennsylvania, California, Florida, New York and Nevada; two Indians among those accused of illegal voting and false citizenship claims
articles.summary: The US Department of Justice has announced charges against 48 non-US citizens in connection with alleged election-related offences across several states,
articles.body: The US Department of Justice has announced charges against 48 non-US citizens in connection with alleged election-related offences across several states, including Pennsylvania, California, Florida, New York and Nevada. The cases involve allegations of illegal voting in federal elections, fraudulent voter registration and falsely claiming US citizenship to register or cast ballots.In a press release issued on October 26, 2026, the department detailed cases filed across multiple federal judicial districts. Several defendants are also accused of making false statements during naturalisation proceedings, including allegedly concealing previous voter registration or voting activity.The department said the cases involve both misdemeanour and felony charges, depending on the alleged offences.Two Indian nationals among those chargedTwo Indian nationals have been named in the announcement. Amandeep Kaur, 30, a lawful permanent resident who is seeking US citizenship, has been accused of registering to vote in December 2022 and voting in the November 2024 US election. The case has been filed in the Central District of California.Kamlesh Navnitlal Shah, 67, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged in the Eastern District of California with voting by a non-citizen. According to the Justice Department, Shah allegedly registered to vote on the day of the November 2024 general election and cast a ballot that day. He has been charged by information.Both individuals face allegations that have yet to be proven in court.Pennsylvania cases involve nine defendantsIn Pennsylvania, nine non-citizens have been charged across two federal judicial districts with allegedly voting in elections involving federal offices.In the Eastern District, the defendants include Alfredo Santiesteban, 73, a Cuban national described as an illegal alien; Artur Kopacz, 50, a Polish national; Osmal Loy, 70, a Cuban national; and Yehuda Peer, 30, an Israeli national. The latter three are identified as lawful permanent residents. Prosecutors allege that the four voted in the 2022 or 2024 general elections.In the Middle District, the defendants include Kenyan nationals Nina Nyawara, 21, and Joyce Donovan, 38; Russian national Inna Henry, 52; Dutch national Joyce Pitts, 80; and Greek national Nourten Kuruju, 64. All are described as lawful permanent residents. The allegations concern voting in federal elections held in 2022 or 2024.California cases include allegations of voter fraud and naturalisation fraudCalifornia accounts for several of the cases detailed by the department, with allegations ranging from illegal voting to false statements in citizenship applications.In the Central District of California, 13 defendants face felony charges, including allegations involving naturalisation applications. They include Belizean national Omar Alexander Munoz, 72, who allegedly registered to vote in 2019 while claiming to be a US citizen and voted in elections in 2020, twice in 2022 and in 2024. He is also accused of making a false statement in his naturalisation application.Other defendants in the district include Salvadoran national Ana Dominguez, 60; Guatemalan national Axel Giovani Prera Garcia, 46; Mexican nationals Flavio Alejandro Zuniga, 43, Ernest Gutierrez Ruvalcaba, 57, Jesus Narez-Madrigal, 52, Jose Antonio Banuelos-Diaz, 42, and Sulema de Leon, 35; Cambodian national Butleng Taing, 43; Honduran national Carlos Antonio Galeas, 54; Pakistani national Muhammad Khan, 50; and Canadian national Rouzbeh Seyamaknejad, 63. The allegations vary and include fraudulent registration, illegal voting and false statements in naturalisation paperwork.In the Eastern District of California, six defendants have been charged with voting by a non-citizen in a federal election. They include Mexican nationals Maricela Nazarin Gonzalez, 43, Camino Giles Jimenez, 51, and Juan Antonio Rivas Garcia, 46; Guatemalan national Rony de Jesus Sicaja, 38; Filipino national Giezell Viduya Adawag, 41; and Indian national Kamlesh Navnitlal Shah, 67.The Justice Department said the offence of voting by a non-citizen in a federal election carries a statutory maximum sentence of one year in federal prison.In the Northern District of California, five defendants face allegations involving illegal voting and false statements during naturalisation proceedings. They are Mexican national Veronica Bullene, 43; Georgian national David Shapiro, 41; Myanmar national Moe Thida Lwin, 57; Tongan national Manakotau Mataele Finau, 61; and Ecuadoran national Maribel del Carmen Garces Barriga, 62.The Southern District of California has four defendants facing allegations of falsely claiming US citizenship to vote, unlawful attempts to obtain naturalisation and false statements under oath. They include Filipino nationals Jose Probitsado Amaro, 51, and Pamele Arbues Line, 56; Canadian national Jennifer Jung, 31; and Guatemalan national Erick Ronaldo Soto Mendizabal, 64.Six defendants charged in FloridaIn the Middle District of Florida, six defendants have been charged with election-related offences. They include Cuban nationals Jamie Orlando Sosa Sardina, 60, and Luis Manuel Perez, 72; Ecuadorian national Martha Haydee Desantis, 81; Canadian nationals Lise Marie Johnson, 69, and Diane Wendy Curley, 55; and Brazilian national Pedro Igor A. Franco, 37.According to the department, Sardina, Desantis and Johnson face allegations of falsely claiming US citizenship to vote and voting illegally. The remaining defendants have been accused of voting by non-citizens. The alleged conduct includes voting in the 2022 and 2024 federal general elections.New York and Nevada casesIn New York, German national Marva Cook, 66, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged in the Northern District with voting by a non-citizen.In the Eastern District of New York, three lawful permanent residents - Irish national Eoin Cranney, 35; Guyanese national Ronald Sheldon Baird, 47; and Jamaican national Karlene Daniels Samuels, 55 - have been charged with voting by non-citizens in federal elections. Prosecutors allege that all three submitted fraudulent voter registration applications and voted in the 2024 general election. The department also said the defendants made admissions about their non-citizen status and voting activity during voluntary interviews with federal agents.In Nevada, Filipino national Jullie Ann Sumalinog Moore, 44, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by a non-citizen in an election involving federal offices, including the presidency and seats in Congress.Charges do not establish guiltThe cases involve allegations of illegal voting, fraudulent voter registration, false claims of US citizenship and misrepresentations in naturalisation proceedings. The charges differ according to the conduct prosecutors allege in each case.The Justice Department clarified that complaints, indictments and information contain allegations rather than findings of guilt. All defendants are presumed innocent unless and until they are proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in court.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A father took his  3-year-old son from Georgia to a New Mexico compound, where the boy died; appeals court overturns relatives’ kidnapping convictions
articles.summary: A federal appeals court has overturned kidnapping convictions in the New Mexico compound case that began when a father took his disabled three-year-old
articles.body: A federal appeals court has overturned kidnapping convictions in the New Mexico compound case that began when a father took his disabled three-year-old son from Georgia. The court held that the jury was misdirected on what makes a kidnapping unlawful, and that the evidence could not show unlawful conduct by the father’s relatives while he held lawful parental rights. Two defendants who represented themselves at trial also had their convictions on separate charges vacated after being wrongly excluded from a key jury discussion. The case centres on the death of Abdul Ghani at a remote desert compound in New Mexico.What the court said happened when a father took his disabled son from his mother in GeorgiaAbdul Ghani was born in August 2014 with hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy, a brain injury caused by a lack of oxygen or blood flow, which delayed his development, according to the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit’s opinion, published by Justia. He also had a form of cerebral palsy and experienced seizures. With medication, therapy and his mother’s care, he had begun speaking and moving independently by the age of three. His mother, Hakima Ramzi, was his primary caregiver, and no one else gave him his medication.The court’s account, drawn from trial testimony and evidence, says his father, Siraj Ibn Wahhaj, came to believe that she was using black magic on the child. That belief rested on messages that a companion, Jany Leveille, claimed to receive from God. Siraj also believed the only remedy was ruqyah, which the opinion describes as a Muslim version of an exorcism. On either 30 November or 1 December 2017, while Ramzi was in the shower, he announced that he was taking the boy to the park. He did not return, and he left the child’s medication behind. A Georgia juvenile court later issued a pick-up order authorising police to retrieve the boy and place him with his mother, but by then he was already in New Mexico.From Alabama to a remote lot in Amalia, where the group built a compound and the boy diedDays after the boy was taken, Siraj, his sisters Hujrah and Subhanah Wahhaj, Subhanah’s husband Lucas Morton, Leveille and the group’s children left Georgia for Alabama. About ten days later they headed for New Mexico. They reached Amalia by 17 December and settled on an empty lot with no water or electricity, where they dug a hole and pushed a trailer into it.According to the opinion, Siraj and Leveille performed ruqyah on the boy every day, in sessions that lasted hours and left him screaming and crying. He died during one such session on 24 December. Leveille then prophesied that he would return as Jesus and lead the group against corrupt institutions, including federal agencies. The adults trained with firearms, built a firing range, hid weapons and dug a tunnel under the compound, where the boy’s body was eventually hidden.On 3 August 2018, the Taos County Sheriff’s Office obtained a warrant to search the compound. Officers arrested Siraj and Lucas and removed the others. One of the children later told officers that the boy’s body was in the tunnel.Why the court reversed kidnapping convictions against the father’s sisters and brother-in-lawFederal law bars unlawfully seizing, confining or carrying away another person, but it exempts a parent who takes his or her own child. Because of that exemption, prosecutors did not charge Siraj with kidnapping. They instead charged Hujrah, Subhanah and Lucas with conspiracy to commit kidnapping and kidnapping resulting in death, and a jury convicted all three.In the opinion issued on 6 October, as published by Justia, Circuit Judge Phillips wrote for a panel that also included Judges McHugh and Moritz. The jury had been told to decide whether the boy was old enough to consent to being taken. If he was not, jurors were to decide whether the taking went against his mother’s consent. The panel concluded that this approach misstated what the law means by an unlawful taking, and it reversed the three kidnapping convictions.A Sixth Amendment violation shut two self-represented defendants out of a jury note discussionThe jury convicted Siraj on three counts, which were, conspiracy to provide material support to kill federal officers, providing that support, and conspiracy to kill federal officers. It convicted Lucas on those counts and on both kidnapping counts, while acquitting Hujrah and Subhanah of the material support charges. The trial court sentenced all four defendants to life imprisonment. Leveille, a fifth defendant, had earlier pleaded guilty to conspiring to provide material support to kill federal officers and to a firearms charge.Siraj and Lucas represented themselves at trial. The trial court excluded them from a conference about a note from the jury, a discussion the appeals court said was of tactical importance. It called this a structural error that violated their Sixth Amendment rights. The court vacated their convictions on the material support and conspiracy-to-kill counts and sent the case back for further proceedings.What the court rejected, from the search of the compound to claims of insufficient evidenceNot every argument succeeded. The court upheld the refusal to suppress evidence seized from the compound, reasoning that the defendants were more like trespassers than tenants on land owned by Jason and Tanya Badger, who had told them to leave. Officers seized firearms, ammunition and a bulletproof vest during the search. The panel also rejected Siraj’s request for a separate trial and treated a challenge to the indictment as waived.On the conspiracy-to-kill charge, the court agreed the jury instructions were wrong because they did not require proof that the intended victims were identified specifically enough to be federal officers. It found no reasonable probability of a different outcome, however. It also held that evidence of a plan to attack federal institutions after the boy’s expected resurrection, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Central Intelligence Agency, was enough to support the charge. A theory about killing any officers who approached the compound was not enough.Because of the reversals, the court did not rule on other claims, including prosecutorial misconduct and whether two of the life sentences were disproportionate.You use AI every day. articles.title: A disused railway tunnel in West Sussex became a winter refuge for rare bats, including a species declared extinct in the UK in 1992
articles.summary: A disused railway tunnel in West Sussex has become a vital winter refuge for rare bats, including the greater mouse-eared bat, which was declared extinct
articles.body: A disused railway tunnel in West Sussex has become a vital winter refuge for rare bats, including the greater mouse-eared bat, which was declared extinct in the UK in 1992. In January 2023, a second bat of this species was discovered hibernating in the same network of tunnels, following the discovery of a lone male there in 2002. According to the National Trust, the tunnel provides an important hibernation site for rare bat species. The discovery highlighted the importance of regular monitoring and safeguarding underground habitats, which offer cool, sheltered and relatively humid conditions for bats during winter.Why is a disused railway tunnel in West Sussex protecting rare batsThe National Trust identifies the disused railway tunnel on one of its West Sussex estates as a vital bat hibernation site containing some rare species. Its guidance on bat conservation explains that underground structures, including cellars, mines, ice-houses and tunnels, provide “sheltered, cool, relatively humid microclimates for hibernating”. These conditions make such places important habitats for bats during the winter months.The tunnel's importance reflects the wider role that existing structures can play in wildlife conservation. Bats use a variety of natural and man-made locations for shelter, including caves, tree cavities, buildings and underground spaces. The National Trust notes that structures such as bridges, houses, churches and barns can also provide suitable roosting places. Protecting these habitats helps maintain places where bats can rest, hibernate and, depending on the site, establish roosts.Why is protecting bat hibernation sites importantThe discovery in West Sussex underlined the need to safeguard the underground site rather than overlook its ecological value. Sheila Wright, a spokesperson for the Sussex Bat Group, said the finding demonstrated the importance of regular monitoring, adding that conservationists could otherwise have missed the discovery of the second greater mouse-eared bat in Britain. She also stressed the importance of protecting the locations used by bats during hibernation.The National Trust's conservation guidance similarly identifies the protection of roosting sites as an important part of its work. The organisation explains that bats face threats associated with the loss of roosts, feeding habitats and, in some cases, direct persecution. Its work includes monitoring bat populations and working with conservation partners, including the Bat Conservation Trust, to assess the condition of habitats on National Trust land. The West Sussex tunnel is one example of an existing underground structure that has value beyond its original transport purpose.Why was the rare bat discovered in SussexThe discovery of the second greater mouse-eared bat raised questions about whether the species might be returning to Britain. According to the BBC, the newly discovered bat was believed to be a vagrant that had crossed the English Channel from France, where an established population exists, before settling in Britain. However, the discovery did not establish whether a breeding population was present in Sussex.Dr Stephanie Murphy of the Sussex Bat Group raised the possibility that a small population might already be recolonising the area without having been detected. She also questioned whether climate change and the UK's increasingly hot summers could be contributing to greater mouse-eared bats moving from mainland Europe. Continued monitoring would help conservationists investigate these possibilities and understand the species' presence in Britain.The tunnel's continued significance demonstrates why disused underground structures can matter to wildlife conservation. The West Sussex rail tunnel is a vital hibernation site for rare bats, while the 2023 discovery showed the importance of regular surveys in detecting animals that might otherwise go unnoticed. Safeguarding such sites and monitoring their wildlife remains an important part of efforts to understand and protect Britain's bat populations.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 2 men charged with national security offences over suspected Iran-linked plot at US air base in UK
articles.summary: Two British men have been charged with national security offences in connection with a suspected plot targeting RAF Fairford, a US-operated military air
articles.body: Two British men have been charged with national security offences in connection with a suspected plot targeting RAF Fairford, a US-operated military air base in western England that has been used by American bombers to strike Iran.Mohmed Ahmad Abdulkarim and Nouman Essghir, both 24 and residents of London, were charged under the National Security Act, the Crown Prosecution Service said on Tuesday. They are expected to appear in court later in the day.Abdulkarim faces a charge of assisting Iran’s intelligence service, while Essghir has been accused of entering a prohibited site for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.Suspected plot led to evacuationsEssghir was arrested outside RAF Fairford on September 27, prompting a major security operation involving armed police and army bomb-disposal experts. Scores of residents were evacuated from nearby homes as authorities searched for explosives.Police later said they had discovered gasoline, an accelerant, in vans at the scene but had found no explosives.Essghir was initially released on bail before being arrested again last week. Abdulkarim was also arrested in the past week. Six other men have been arrested and released on bail as the investigation continues.The incident prompted US authorities to withdraw their bombers from RAF Fairford amid concerns over a potential Iranian-linked threat.British authorities have linked Tehran to the suspected plot. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the incident was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard. Iran has denied involvement, though it has previously maintained that military bases used to attack its territory could be considered legitimate targets.MI5 warns of rising Iran-linked threatsThe arrests come amid warnings from British intelligence officials about an increase in threats linked to foreign states.Earlier this month, MI5 director general Ken McCallum warned that Iran and Russia were expanding their hostile activities in the UK. He said Tehran was seeking to widen its targets beyond Iranians opposed to the country's Islamic authorities.McCallum said more than 50 people had been arrested over Iran-linked plots in the past year.Laurence Taylor, assistant commissioner and head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK, said authorities were working to identify and counter threats believed to be directed by Iran.“We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state,” Taylor said, adding that authorities were working together to respond to the threat.You use AI every day. articles.title: Flavio Bolsonaro flees to US after election defeat, vows to challenge Lula's victory: Report
articles.summary: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday's presidential runoff to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, left the country for the United States,
articles.body: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday's presidential runoff to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, left the country for the United States, an ally told news agency Reuters on Tuesday, confirming an earlier media report.His reported departure came after Brazil's Supreme Court ordered him to surrender his passports within 24 hours as part of a money-laundering investigation, in which he denies wrongdoing. Brazilian authorities cancelled his passports on Tuesday after he missed the deadline.The reported move has drawn comparisons with his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who travelled to the US after refusing to concede defeat to Lula in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro later returned to Brazil and was sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup.Flavio has yet to formally concede defeat, saying he would seek to annul the election result over alleged voter irregularities. His Liberal Party, however, acknowledged Lula's victory on Monday.Lula secured more than 64 million votes, defeating Bolsonaro, who received just under 60 million, by nearly 4.4 million votes. The incumbent is expected to take office on January 5, 2027, for a fourth non-consecutive term.A key factor in Lula’s comeback was the mobilisation of voters who had abstained in the first round or backed other candidates. An additional 14.1 million voters participated in the runoff, with analysts estimating that three-quarters of these votes went to Lula.Central to the campaign was lawmaker André Janones’ WhatsApp channel, “Lula’s Army”, which attracted nearly 11 million people and encouraged supporters to campaign on social media.Bolsonaro has pledged to organise opposition to Lula and seek to nullify the results. He said, “I am going to gather elected lawmakers and senators to organize our strategy and make the lower house and the Senate our fortress against barbaric acts that are set to happen in another four years of Lula.”However, overturning the result would require evidence of fraud affecting Lula’s 4.4 million-vote margin and approval from Brazil’s eight-member electoral court before certification on December 18.Benjamin Gedan, director of the Stimson Center’s Latin America programme, warned, “False claims of fraud are becoming commonplace, though that does not make them any less dangerous.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Denver voters rejected development on a 155-acre former golf course in 2023; after a land swap and $70 million bond allocation, the city is moving to permanently protect it as a public park
articles.summary: Denver is moving ahead with plans to turn the former Park Hill Golf Course into a major public green space, appointing a prominent landscape architecture
articles.body: Denver is moving ahead with plans to turn the former Park Hill Golf Course into a major public green space, appointing a prominent landscape architecture firm to lead its design while taking steps to safeguard the property against future development. The decision follows years of debate over the site’s future, culminating in a 2023 vote in which Denver residents rejected a proposal to develop the land. The announcement was reported by Axios Denver and The Denver Gazette on October 13, 2026. Both outlets said Mayor Mike Johnston had selected Michael Van Valkenburgh Associates (MVVA) to oversee the design of the 155-acre Park Hill Park, with the city also pursuing formal protections to preserve the land for public use. The project marks a significant stage in the transformation of a former golf course into a regional park intended to serve residents across Denver.A new future for a contested siteLocated in northeast Denver, the property operated as a golf course from the 1930s until its closure in 2018. Its future became a subject of public debate after the former owner explored plans for a mixed-use development.In 2023, voters rejected a development measure by 58.8% to 42.2%, reinforcing opposition to converting the site into a commercial and residential project. A conservation easement dating to the late 1990s had also restricted the property’s use, meaning a change in its purpose required voter approval. Denver subsequently pursued a land exchange with Westside Investment Partners, the company that owned the former golf course. Under the agreement approved by the City Council in 2025 and The Denver Gazette’s May 13, 2025 report, “Denver City Council OKs Park Hill land swap to create fourth-largest park,” the deal involved exchanging 145 acres of city-owned land in Adams County, near Denver International Airport, and providing approximately $12.7 million from the Denver Parks Legacy Fund as part of the transaction.A landscape shaped around ColoradoMVVA will lead the park’s design, bringing experience from major public-space projects across the United States. Its portfolio includes Brooklyn Bridge Park in New York City, Gathering Place in Tulsa, the grounds surrounding the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago and the transformation of the former rail corridor now known as The 606.The firm’s selection followed a competitive process that attracted interest from landscape architecture practices around the world. Founder Michael Van Valkenburgh is expected to take an active role in the project. The design will build on public consultation and a framework developed by Denver Parks & Recreation. Plans identify potential features such as athletic fields, sports courts, playgrounds, walking and cycling trails, water features, natural areas and a field house. Existing stormwater detention ponds are also incorporated into the preferred site plan.Water conservation is expected to be an important consideration. The landscape concept calls for a distinctly Colorado character, with an emphasis on native and drought-tolerant plants suited to the region’s climate. The aim is to balance active recreation with open space and opportunities for visitors to experience the natural landscape.Funding and the road aheadThe park carries an estimated budget of $100 million, although the full funding plan has not yet been finalised. Denver voters approved $70 million for Park Hill Park through the city’s $950 million Vibrant Denver Bond programme in 2025. The bond funding is expected to support the design contract, the cost of which was still being negotiated as of October 13. The City Council is expected to consider the contract later this year.Design work is scheduled to continue through 2027, with construction expected to begin in June 2028. City officials have indicated that the park could open to the public in 2029, although the construction schedule and whether parts of the site will remain accessible during the work have yet to be settled.Protecting the land for public useAlongside the design process, Denver plans to formally designate Park Hill as parkland. The measure would strengthen protections against future development by requiring voter approval before the property could be sold or disposed of. The designation is intended to provide long-term certainty after years of disagreement over whether the land should become a development site or remain open space.Park Hill Park is already managed by Denver Parks & Recreation and has begun welcoming visitors. The next phase will focus on turning the broad vision for the property into a detailed design, with public input continuing to inform decisions about its facilities and layout. For Denver, the project represents both the redevelopment of a large urban site and an effort to preserve land for shared public use for generations to come.You use AI every day. articles.title: A 41-acre California vineyard estate owned by the family trust of heart surgeon Thomas Fogarty has sold for $11.04 million; the property has a 14,500 sq. ft. Italian villa with wine-tasting room, home theatre and spa
articles.summary: The 41-acre vineyard estate in Portola Valley, owned by the Fogarty Family Trust associated with the late cardiovascular surgeon and Thomas Fogarty Winery
articles.body: The 41-acre vineyard estate in Portola Valley, owned by the Fogarty Family Trust associated with the late cardiovascular surgeon and Thomas Fogarty Winery founder Dr Thomas J. Fogarty, sold for $11.04 million in September, the Mountain View Voice reported. The property includes a three-level stone Italian villa with breathtaking views of San Francisco Bay. The initial asking price was $15.5 million, according to the listing on Kavanaugh Real Estate.The Italian villaThe main house is a 14,500-square-foot villa built mostly of stone. The house spans three levels linked by an elevator, with six bedrooms and nine full bathrooms, according to the listing.The entrance opens onto a foyer with sightlines to the Bay, and a gallery beside it houses an entertainment bar beneath a barrel-vaulted ceiling. The living room has a coffered all-wood ceiling and three sets of French doors leading to a terrace, while the dining room has two sets of French doors and a butler’s pantry with warming drawers.The main suite is upstairs and is the largest private space in the home, according to the listing. It begins with a sitting room featuring a wet bar and a private balcony, followed by a wood-panelled office with a Bay-view balcony and a gas-log fireplace. The bedroom includes a dressing area with a walk-in wardrobe, while its two bathrooms feature a sunken jetted tub beneath body sprays, two rainspout showers and a cedar sauna.The kitchen has two islands, one topped with butcher’s block and the other with granite. It is equipped with commercial-quality appliances, including a six-burner Thermador gas range, a double grill, a pot filler, warming drawers, a sink and a wok burner. Gaggenau ovens and a steamer, a Miele dishwasher, and a Sub-Zero wine cooler, refrigerator and freezer complete the setup. Beside it is the breakfast room, with a coffered wood-panelled ceiling and a raised fireplace. It opens onto an aviary that can also be accessed from outside. A den with oak panelling and built-in shelving has glass doors that fully retract onto the front terrace. The family room, beyond the living room, has a wood stove set in a precast mantel. Two bedrooms on the main level each open onto the grounds. Two more upstairs suites, one customised as an office, each have an en suite bathroom.This is more than a typical family home. The villa’s lower level is dedicated to entertaining and wellness. There is a theatre with seating for eight and a retractable screen. A tasting area with a copper-topped wet bar sits beside a wine cellar behind iron-and-glass doors. A spa bathroom features a large jetted tub, a cedar sauna and a steam room. The house also includes a dog-bathing room, two laundry rooms, a formal powder room with trompe-l’œil finishes, a security alarm and a backup generator. Outside, the grounds feature a swimming pool, a pool house with a full kitchen and bathroom, and a tennis court. The setting is built for entertaining, and the scale reflects that.A family estateThe estate belonged to the Fogarty Family Trust, which is associated with Dr Thomas J. Fogarty, a longtime Portola Valley resident who founded Thomas Fogarty Winery. He died before the sale, and his name remains attached to the vineyard and the wine label.Winemaking was part of the family story. The estate served as a working property as well as a home, and that history gives the sale a personal dimension that a standard real estate transaction cannot offer.Portola Valley has long attracted people looking to trade the bustle of the valley floor for acreage in the hills. The listing described the property as the “perfect place to escape from the fast daily pace of Silicon Valley”.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: No entry into Agamic temples for non-Hindus sporting religious markers, rules Madras high court
articles.summary: MADURAI: Non-Hindus who sport their religious markers -- and who do not subscribe to their reverence to the deity -- cannot be permitted to enter the
articles.body: MADURAI: Non-Hindus who sport their religious markers -- and who do not subscribe to their reverence to the deity -- cannot be permitted to enter the Agamic Hindu temple premises, Madras high court has held.A division bench of Justice G R Swaminathan and Justice P Murugan, hearing a public interest litigation filed by K Thangam Venkatesh of Madurai, said: “The petitioner is a Hindu. He is entitled to insist that the trustees of the various agamic temples in Tamil Nadu uphold the agamic injunctions by not permitting non-Hindus who do not sign the undertaking from crossing the flagpole. If such entry is permitted, it would defile the sanctity of the temple. We intend to go a step further. Even entry into the temple premises, cannot be permitted for non-Hindus who sport their religious markers and who do not subscribe their reverence for the deity concerned. This subscription must be in the format prescribed by the institution concerned."In this regard the judges flayed Badrudeen Mustafa, a TVK MLA from Madurai Central constituency, as he was seen inside the Meenakshi temple for ‘inspection’ and was atop the gopuram during its recent consecration.“We notice in recent times that there are egregious breaches. Badrudeen Mustafa, an MLA representing the Madurai Central constituency, where the famed Meenakshi temple is located, went inside the temple premises soon after his election. He claimed that he had a right to inspect if proper amenities were being provided. He also went up the temple towers on the occasion of Kumbabishekam. It is ironic that the said MLA proclaimed that Sanatana Dharma ought to be eradicated,” observed the judges.“We take judicial notice of a video doing rounds in the social media of persons wearing skull caps, pushing their way through in Tiruvannamalai Arunachaleswarar temple, notwithstanding the vigorous protests of the devotees. The HR and CE staff stood as mute spectators,” the judges said."We take judicial notice of the fact that a minister who is a Christian by faith, entered Thiruchendur temple without giving the undertaking required from non-Hindus,” they added.They, however, commended Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay, saying: “We have the illustrious instance of chief minister C Joseph Vijay, who worshipped Goddess Meenakshi after signing the undertaking. The chief minister, who is a Christian by faith, was not asked to convert to Hinduism. He was only requested to affirm his reverence for the deity. This is what we call an inclusive approach."Flaying ‘Chamchagiri’ in politics, the division bench said, “not only Chamchagiri, but also optics matters in a democracy. We know of one political leader, who is a fundamentalist subscribing to a non-Hindu faith. But he would make it a point to visit the temple and also prominently display the religious mark on his forehead. This was to play to the gallery. The vote value of such a display is obvious. We hold that usages and customs of the temple cannot kneel down before such display of Chamchagiri and optics.”The PIL, filed by K Thangam Venkatesh, sought a direction to the authorities to conduct inquiry against violators of statutory provisions of Tamil Nadu Temple Entry Authorization Act and the Rules and strictly enforce the statutory provisions.While passing the orders, the judges made it clear at the very outset that the scope of the judgment was confined to Agamic temples. “Lord Ayyapa has devotees cutting across religions. Shirdi Sai Baba is also beyond religion. Both Hindus as well as Muslims claimed him as their own. Of course, now, he is more a part of the Hindu pantheon,” they observed.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chennai | Silver Rate in Chennai | Bank Holidays in Chennai | Public Holidays in Chennai | Chennai AQI | Weather in Chennai | Petrol Price in Chennai | Diesel Price in Chennai | CNG Price in Chennai | LPG Price in ChennaiStay updated with the latest Chennai news. articles.title: In 2024, Colin Farrell launched a foundation inspired by his son James; by 2026, it had selected 16 US organisations for grants of $10,000 to $50,000 to help adults with intellectual disabilities
articles.summary: For many families, planning for a child with an intellectual or developmental disability to transition into adulthood brings difficult questions about
articles.body: For many families, planning for a child with an intellectual or developmental disability to transition into adulthood brings difficult questions about housing, employment, healthcare and long-term support. Actor Colin Farrell has helped bring attention to these challenges through a foundation inspired by his son James, who has Angelman syndrome, a rare neurogenetic condition. By 2026, the Colin Farrell Foundation had selected 16 organisations across the United States for grants ranging from approximately $10,000 to $50,000 each. According to Sayrs Consulting, which oversaw the foundation’s inaugural grant programme, the selected projects focus on practical solutions designed to improve independence, inclusion and quality of life.Foundation inspired by Farrell’s son JamesFarrell launched the Colin Farrell Foundation in 2024 to support individuals and families living with intellectual and developmental disabilities. His son James was born with Angelman syndrome, a condition that can affect movement, communication and development. The actor has spoken publicly about the importance of ensuring that James and other people with disabilities have opportunities to live meaningful lives with dignity, connection and appropriate support. The foundation’s mission reflects concerns shared by families who must plan for their children’s needs as they grow older.According to the foundation’s official website, its work centres on education, awareness, advocacy and innovative programmes. Its broader priorities include accessible housing, day programmes, employment opportunities and support for the people who provide direct care. The foundation’s first donation was recorded in August 2024, followed by its inaugural fundraiser in Chicago in December that year. These early efforts helped establish the organisation and prepare the ground for its first major grantmaking initiative.Sixteen organisations selected from 236 applicationsThe foundation’s inaugural Innovation Grant programme for 2025-2026 attracted 236 applications from organisations working with people with intellectual and developmental disabilities across the country. According to Sayrs Consulting, an independent review committee assessed the applications and selected 16 organisations whose proposals received the highest overall scores. The grants range from approximately $10,000 to $50,000, depending on the selected projects. The programme was designed to support organisations addressing gaps in services that can become particularly challenging when young people with disabilities leave school-based programmes, often around the age of 22.After school services end, families may have to navigate a fragmented system to find suitable housing, structured daytime activities, healthcare and inclusive employment. Community organisations frequently provide these services, but their capacity and resources vary. The foundation’s grants are intended to strengthen these existing organisations and help them develop approaches that could be expanded or replicated in other communities.Housing, employment and independent living are prioritiesThe 16 selected organisations work across several areas, including accessible housing, vocational training, recreation, life-skills development and community participation. In North Carolina, 3 Bluebirds Farm operates a social enterprise designed to build life skills and provide inclusive employment opportunities for young adults with autism. A New Leaf in Oklahoma focuses on integrated housing and vocational services to help people develop greater independence.Independence Landing in Florida is developing culinary workforce training alongside residential opportunities for adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities. In California, Golden Heart Ranch uses gardening activities through its “We Grow Together” programme to encourage skills development and a sense of belonging. Other recipients are working to expand accessible recreation and social connections. The Ability Center of Southern Nevada operates an adaptive fitness centre with a sensory gym and training programmes, while Jacob’s Chance in Virginia provides inclusive sports and social activities.Community Access to the Arts in Massachusetts supports artistic expression through workshops and performances, giving people with disabilities opportunities to share their work and participate in cultural life. These projects illustrate the programme’s broad approach: support is not limited to medical or residential care but also includes work, recreation, creativity and relationships.Grants address gaps in adult disability servicesOther selected organisations are focusing on housing models and coordinated support. L’Arche Chicago works to foster community living with nursing support, while Sweetwater Spectrum in California develops a residential model designed around inclusive community life. Tall Tales Ranch in Colorado combines housing, employment and storytelling. The Next Step Programs in Pennsylvania helps young adults access integrated housing and employment pathways. Villa Esperanza Services in California provides education, speech services and community programmes.Meanwhile, Equip Services in Alabama is expanding vocational training and access through a wheelchair-accessible van. Emory Valley Center in Tennessee is developing pathways towards greater community independence, and Many Hands Lifesharing Community in Michigan combines farming, crafts and day programmes. SNACK and Friends, a New York nonprofit supporting young people with autism and other developmental disabilities, is piloting transitional housing and enrichment for young people with significant intellectual and developmental disabilities. Together, the projects reflect the foundation’s focus on giving people opportunities to participate in their communities while providing families with additional support.A national effort to strengthen community supportThe grant programme marks an important step in the foundation’s effort to support established organisations rather than relying on a single model of care. Its priorities include affordable shared housing, inclusive employment, accessible technologies and partnerships between public agencies, private organisations and nonprofits. The foundation’s work also highlights a challenge that extends beyond individual families: ensuring that services remain available as people with disabilities move into adulthood.For Farrell, the initiative builds on a personal connection to the disability community while supporting organisations working on practical solutions across the United States. Singing pumpkins, skeletons and spooky figures provide the visual centrepiece, while smoke effects and projected clips add to the atmosphere.One of the most distinctive features is Zero, the ghost dog from The Nightmare Before Christmas, which appears to fly around the house’s chimney. The film also features prominently on a screen facing the street, including its familiar Halloween-themed musical sequence.The display includes skeletal versions of Disney princesses and other recognisable characters, alongside villains from the Harry Potter series. Photo opportunities and additional decorations along the Wardlow Road side of the property give visitors more to explore beyond the main performance. His experience with technical systems, combined with his interest in music, sound production and theatrical lighting, helped shape the display into a computer-controlled show.He is also a musician who has performed with brass ensembles and played instruments including bagpipes. His background in recording and editing sound has contributed to the way music and visual effects are integrated into the production.Ann Haberman spent decades working at Disneyland’s Blue Bayou Restaurant, located inside the Pirates of the Caribbean attraction. Her long association with the theme park adds another connection to the world of immersive entertainment. Both are Long Beach natives, and their annual displays have become a shared creative project. New decorations and effects are added over time, giving returning visitors something different to discover.Why families keep coming backThe appeal extends beyond the elaborate technology. Their display relies on creativity and technical expertise, but its wider appeal comes from giving people a reason to step outside and share a seasonal experience.A Christmas show is nextHalloween is only one part of the Habermans’ annual tradition. articles.title: Farmers lock naib tehsildar's office in Kurukshetra over ‘wrong paddy data’
articles.summary: Farmers in Kurukshetra locked the naib tehsildar’s office over alleged wrong paddy data on a govt portal; SDM assured corrections by Wednesday 2 pm.
articles.body: Kurukshetra: Farmers protesting alleged errors in paddy-related data uploaded on govt portal locked the naib tehsildar’s office at the New Mini Secretariat here on Tuesday. The protest, led by the Bharatiya Kisan Union (Shaheed Bhagat Singh), continued for nearly two hours before the farmers unlocked the office after SDM Aman Kumar assured them the issue would be resolved by 2 pm on Wednesday.The farmers reached the office around 11.30 am, carrying a chain and lock. They locked the office and staged a sit-in outside, raising slogans against the administration over alleged discrepancies in crop and land records.Sanjay Nambardar, district president of the union, alleged that revenue officials had entered incorrect information on the portal without physically visiting the fields. He claimed that officials sent farmers from one office to another without resolving the issue.According to the union, discrepancies in paddy and land records in a single patwar circle had affected farmers from around 20 villages, preventing them from selling their produce at mandis.Sanjay alleged that incorrect data was uploaded for more than 50 farmers. In some cases, non-basmati paddy was recorded as basmati, while agricultural land was incorrectly marked as barren.He said these discrepancies create difficulties for farmers trying to sell their produce and obtain gate passes at procurement centres.The farmers claimed they had been visiting the offices of the SDM, tehsildar and patwari for nearly 20 days to get their records corrected. They also submitted a complaint during a grievance redressal camp, but the issue remained unresolved.The protesters alleged that officials kept referring them to other departments instead of correcting the errors on the portal.Ravinder Singh, a farmer, said the portal initially recorded non-basmati paddy on his nearly 13 acres of land. However, the records later showed around seven acres under basmati paddy, while nearly two acres were marked as barren.He said the incorrect entries created hurdles in selling his crop and obtaining a gate pass.Before reaching the New Mini Secretariat, the farmers assembled near Shaheed Udham Singh Chowk on KDB Road and took out a protest march to the administrative complex. They then locked the naib tehsildar’s office and staged a sit-in outside.Following the intervention of officials, SDM Aman Kumar heard the farmers’ grievances and assured them that the incorrect data would be rectified by 2 pm on Wednesday. articles.title: Israel election exit polls show no clear winner as Netanyahu and rivals fall short of majority
articles.summary: Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party is projected to emerge as the largest party in the Knesset, but opposition parties led by Gadi
articles.body: Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party is projected to emerge as the largest party in the Knesset, but opposition parties led by Gadi Eisenkot are ahead as a bloc, with neither side securing a clear path to a parliamentary majority, according to exit polls by Channels 12, 13 and public broadcaster Kan.Kan projects Likud to win 25 seats and Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party 21. It puts the anti-Netanyahu bloc at 53 seats, compared with 50 for the Netanyahu-led bloc. Arab-led parties, which oppose Netanyahu but are not part of the Zionist anti-Netanyahu bloc, are projected to win 17 seats.Channel 13 projects Likud to win 25 seats and Yashar 23. It puts the anti-Netanyahu bloc at 53 seats, compared with 50 for the right-wing religious bloc supporting the prime minister. Arab-led parties are projected to win a record 17 seats.Channel 12’s exit poll gives Likud 24 seats and Yashar 22. It projects the bloc of Jewish-led parties opposing Netanyahu to win 52 seats, against 50 for parties supporting him, while Arab-led parties are expected to secure a record 18 seats.Neither camp is close to the 61 seats required for a majority in the 120-member Knesset. The projections suggest that coalition negotiations could stretch over the coming days and weeks, with Arab-led parties potentially playing a role in efforts to form a government, despite generally not having joined governing coalitions.Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot could seek the first opportunity to form a government by appealing to President Isaac Herzog. Netanyahu leads the largest individual party, while Eisenkot heads the bloc projected to have more seats overall.The results also leave open the possibility that neither side will be able to assemble a coalition, potentially forcing Israel into another election. Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister in the interim. The scenario would echo the period from 2019 to 2022, when Israel held five rounds of voting.Former prime minister Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad party is projected to finish third. Kan and Channel 13 give it 14 seats, while Channel 12 projects 12. The Arab-led Joint List and the left-wing Democrats are projected to win 10 seats each in Kan’s poll, while Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu is projected to win eight.Kan projects the far-right Otzma Yehudit and the Islamist Ra’am parties to win seven seats each. The ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and United Torah Judaism, along with Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism, are each projected to win six seats.All three exit polls project that the nonaligned Reservists party and the right-wing People of Israel party will fall short of the 3.25% threshold required to enter the Knesset.The Central Elections Committee has begun counting votes and is expected to release official tallies through the night. articles.title: In 2017, Jake Gyllenhaal bought a New York apartment in an 1882 bookbinding factory for $8.63 million; eight years later, he sold it for $14 million while the building faced a $376 million lawsuit
articles.summary: In downtown Manhattan, celebrity real estate often comes with a peculiar combination of history, discretion and extraordinary price tags.
articles.body: In downtown Manhattan, celebrity real estate often comes with a peculiar combination of history, discretion and extraordinary price tags. Jake Gyllenhaal’s latest property move checks all three boxes. After eight years at one of Tribeca’s most coveted addresses, the Oscar-nominated actor has sold his apartment at 443 Greenwich Street for $14 million, turning a 2017 purchase into a substantial gain while the landmark building remains embroiled in a major legal dispute.From bookbinding factory to celebrity enclaveAccording to Realtor and Architectural Digest, the building dates to 1882, when it operated as a bookbinding factory. Its industrial past remains visible through architectural details incorporated into the luxury condominium, including exposed wooden beams, mahogany windows, antique bronze doors and other historic elements.The conversion transformed the property into a 53-unit residential building that has become particularly attractive to celebrities seeking privacy in Manhattan.Gyllenhaal purchased his apartment in an off-market transaction in 2017 for approximately $8.63 million, according to Realtor. Eight years later, the 2,868-square-foot residence has changed hands for $14 million, representing a gain of more than $5 million before accounting for transaction costs and other expenses.Inside Gyllenhaal’s former residenceThe fifth-floor apartment combines the scale of a downtown loft with the amenities expected from a luxury condominium. Realtor reports that the residence features three bedrooms, three bathrooms, a chef's kitchen and an open-plan layout.Across the building, the residences retain a sense of the property's industrial character while introducing contemporary finishes. Architectural Digest highlights features such as white oak flooring, custom metal wall panels and grand entry foyers.The building's amenities extend well beyond individual residences. Residents have access to an underground parking garage, private elevators, a resident-only courtyard and extensive security and concierge services. A 71-foot indoor swimming pool, gym, Turkish bath, landscaped courtyard and rooftop terrace further reinforce the property's luxury credentials, according to Realtor.A magnet for famous residentsGyllenhaal was hardly the first celebrity to be drawn to 443 Greenwich Street. Realtor reports that the building has been associated with stars including Jennifer Lawrence, Harry Styles, Blake Lively and Ryan Reynolds, Mike Myers, Justin Timberlake and Lewis Hamilton.Its privacy has been a major part of its appeal. Private entrances, underground access and elevators that open directly to residences allow high-profile residents to move through the building with limited exposure.Residences are often owned by trusts or LLCs, reflecting their low profile. Gyllenhaal's apartment was similarly purchased through an entity connected to his business manager.A $376 million legal battleGyllenhaal's profitable sale comes as the condominium itself faces a significant legal controversy. According to Realtor and Architectural Digest, the building's condo board filed a $376 million lawsuit in 2021 against developer Nate Berman's Metro Loft and architecture firm CetraRuddy.The complaint alleges breach of contract, construction defects and code violations. Among the issues cited are leaks throughout the building, problems with the courtyard's drainage system and improperly installed brickwork.The developer and architect have denied the allegations, and the litigation remains ongoing.For Gyllenhaal, however, the latest chapter at 443 Greenwich Street is a completed real-estate transaction. His departure leaves behind one of Manhattan's most recognizable celebrity residential addresses, even as its blend of industrial history, modern luxury and high-profile residents continues to define its appeal.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and RealtorReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.body: The historic World’s End pub in Tilbury, Essex, was almost destroyed by a fire on 23 September 2026, prompting concern over the loss of a landmark associated with Samuel Pepys and Daniel Defoe. The Grade II listed building was included in Thurrock’s recently launched heritage trails and was recognised for its connection to the town’s naval history. According to Essex Police, officers were called to the former pub on Fort Road shortly after 4.40 pm and arrested a man in his 20s on suspicion of arson. Police attended the scene and arrested a man in his 20s on suspicion of arson. The force said the man remained in custody for questioning as the investigation continued. Police also appealed for information, including CCTV footage, dashcam recordings and other material that could help establish the circumstances surrounding the fire.In an official statement Thurrock Council issued the following day, the fire had destroyed the pub, describing the damage as extensive. In its statement published on 24 September, the council said local councillors had expressed their sadness over the loss of the historic building. Essex Police asked anyone with relevant information to quote incident 918 of 23 September when contacting the force. The investigation was ongoing at the time of the statements, and the arrest did not establish the cause of the fire or determine responsibility for it.How was the World’s End pub linked to Samuel Pepys and Daniel DefoeThe World’s End pub had historical associations with two notable English figures: Samuel Pepys, the diarist whose writings document aspects of seventeenth-century life, and Daniel Defoe, the author known for works including Robinson Crusoe and Moll Flanders. Thurrock Council’s Cabinet Member for Veterans, Enforcement and Environment, Councillor Russell Cherry, referred to these connections in his response to the fire.Cherry said the pub had been frequented by Defoe and visited by Pepys, who recorded his visit in his diary. These historical links made the building a recognisable part of Tilbury’s heritage. The council also highlighted the pub’s connection to the town’s naval past, placing it among the sites that visitors could explore through the borough’s heritage trails. The building therefore featured not only as a local pub but also as a site associated with the area’s historical development and notable visitors.Why was the World’s End pub important to Tilbury’s heritage trailsThe World’s End pub was a Grade II listed building that had stood for centuries, according to Tilbury St Chads ward councillor Bailey Scott. Its location and historical associations connected it with Tilbury’s wider heritage, including the area’s naval history. Thurrock Council described the building as a tangible link to the town’s past and noted that it had recently been included in the borough’s heritage trails.The heritage trails were launched in the week before the fire, according to Cherry’s statement. In his statement, he said: “Thurrock has an incredible heritage and the World’s End is an important part of that, so I was terribly sorry to learn of the fire which has all but destroyed it.” He also referred to the pub’s place in the newly launched heritage trails and its historical associations with Defoe and Pepys.Cherry said he hoped the site would recover from the fire and that another pub would be built there. He noted that the building had been destroyed by fire previously and subsequently recovered. His comments set out the council’s hope for the site’s future, although the statement did not confirm that a rebuilding plan had been approved or that restoration work would begin.Scott also expressed sadness at the destruction of the historic pub, highlighting its importance to local residents. He described the Grade II listed building as a place that had held generations of memories for people in Tilbury. Scott thanked Essex County Fire and Rescue Service and other emergency services for their efforts in tackling the fire. He also acknowledged the Port of Tilbury Police for their response and assistance in keeping the public safe.What do police know about the fire at the historic World’s End pubEssex Police confirmed that a man in his 20s had been arrested on suspicion of arson and that he remained in custody for questioning when the force issued its statement on 24 September 2026. The police investigation was continuing, and officers appealed for anyone with relevant footage or information to come forward. Thurrock Council also stated that it understood Essex County Fire and Rescue Service was investigating the cause of the blaze.The council expressed hope that the World’s End site would recover and that a new pub could eventually be built there. articles.title: Drunk driver Ishan Pandhare mowed down two California Polytechnic State University students, left them like 'garbage in the roadway', alleges lawsuit
articles.summary: A lawsuit has revealed a heinous overspeeding case in California that took place earlier this year when two 19-year-old students of California Polytechnic
articles.body: A lawsuit has revealed a heinous overspeeding case in California that took place earlier this year when two 19-year-old students of California Polytechnic State University, Lilianne Burke and Zoey Archibald, were mowed down by a speeding Tesla driven by allegedly drunk Ishan Pandhare, a 20-year-old former student of Cal Poly. The accident took place on January 8 and the lawsuit was filed in July. Pandhare is one of the several defendants named in the complaint. The lawsuit seeks monetary damages for the serious physical injuries of the girls and their emotional distress. Pandhare has been accused of attending multiple alcohol parties before hitting the sorority sisters at 60mph in a 25-mph zone.Pandhare also faces charges of DUI causing bodily injury, reckless driving causing injury and hit-and run causing injury or death in a separate case in which he has pleaded not guilty.According to court documents, Pandhare attended a party hosted by a 21-year-old and then another event hosted by Kappa Sigma fraternity members. Witnesses said he was visibly drunk and his speech was also slurring. After the crash, Pandhare told the police that he did not do anything illegal, and he was not drunk. "Two Cal Poly students were run over and left bleeding in the road by an underage driver under the influence who cowardly fled the scene," Theo Emison, Archibald's attorney, told The San Luis Obispo Tribune. "We will find all persons who are responsible in any way for this tragedy and hold every one of them accountable for this despicable conduct.""There are so many layers of failure here that had the law been followed by any one of the people who furnished the alcohol, provided the vehicle, encouraged excessive consumption and drove the vehicle, this life-changing collision would not have happened," Christopher Dolan, Burke's attorney, told The Tribune.'Left like run-over garbage'The lawsuit claims Pandhare never used the brakes or made any attempt to slow down before or after the accident, leaving the women with injuries so severe they required surgery and continued treatment. The sisters were "left like run over garbage in the roadway," and had to be immediately transported to the hospital, according to the lawsuit.One witness said the two victims flew through the air after being hit by Pandhare.The two students also sued the Kapp Sigma fraternity for encouraging underage students to drink.After being suspended from Cal Poly and posting his $150,000 bail, Pandhare has been living in San Diego with his parents. He was present in court on Monday, with his mother and father sitting in the gallery to support him, the Tribune reported.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
